item.title: Truth under pressure: Life as an investigative journalist in Kyrgyzstan | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
What does it mean to practice investigative journalism in Kyrgyzstan? What are the consequences of holding politicians accountable for corruption? Here, practicing journalism can be life-threatening.
Instead of being celebrated as heroes, journalists in the Central Asian republic of Kyrgyzstan often face threats. Their private lives suffer, as does their safety—and sometimes even their very lives wind up on the line. Ali Toktakunov, one of Kyrgyzstan’s best-known investigative journalists, stands up to the ruling elite by exposing a corruption case. But when his most important informant is shot dead, Toktakunov flees to the Czech Republic. The tension between his personal life and his work is brought to light by director Samara Sagynbaeva—who is also his wife. Her diary-style documentary paints a portrait of a courageous journalist. At the same time, the film serves as a reminder of the fragility of democracy and the rule of law in a country where freedom of expression is by no means a given.

item.title: The Social Reckoning That Wasn't
item.author: Patrick Boyle
item.content:encoded:
Go to https://surfshark.com/boyle or use code BOYLE at checkout to get 4 extra months of Surfshark!
Last month Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion dollars to settle claims that it knowingly harmed teenagers — a number the press immediately called Big Tech's "tobacco moment." Wall Street responded by sending the stock up.
In this video I read the actual 130-page consent judgment so that you don't have to, and work out what Meta really bought for its money. It turns out the headline figure is worth about two days of revenue, the "new" safety rules are mostly settings Meta had already written for itself, and the fine print lands rather more heavily on TikTok than on Meta. We'll also get into why the attorneys general took the deal, what Meta was actually paying to make disappear, and why the real reckoning might end up happening in a cinema rather than a courtroom.

item.title: Laughing to survive - On tour with the Palestine Comedy Club | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Six Palestinian comedians go on tour in Israel and the Palestinian territories. What begins as a stand-up comedy show evolves, in the face of terror and war, into a plea for humanity.
Although there are no comedy clubs -- and hardly any stand-up comedy -- in the Palestinian territories, comedian Alaa Shehada decides to found a stand-up comedy troupe, along with other local artists. Their goal? To develop a program that combines Western comedic traditions with Palestinian narrative forms, to perform in front of an audience.
Despite cultural and security hurdles, the group’s six members—each holding a different travel permit—manage to stage a tour of theaters in the Palestinian territories and in Israel. The shows are well attended, and the group begins to gain attention, even internationally.
Eventually, they receive an invitation to London for a series of performances. These are set to begin on, of all days, October 7, 2023. Against the backdrop of Hamas’ terrorist attack on Israel and the ensuing war in Gaza, the comedians face the challenge of performing before an increasingly polarized audience in the UK.
Palestine Comedy Club is a film about the search for humor in everyday life under excruciating conditions—and the attempt to forge connections through shared laughter.

item.title: San Bernardino Train Crash: What Caused This 100mph Runaway Train?
item.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
item.content:encoded:
On May 12, 1989, Southern Pacific freight train 7551 rocketed down California’s Cajon Pass at over 100 mph before derailing into a San Bernardino neighborhood. Caused by fatal weight miscalculations and failing brakes, the crash killed four people and destroyed seven homes. But thirteen days later, a second catastrophe struck the exact same street when a damaged underground pipeline ruptured, igniting a massive inferno. This documentary investigates the series of tragic human errors, mechanical failures, and oversight lapses that led to one of the most disastrous chain reactions in American transportation history.

item.title: Black people in Nazi Germany - Lionel Romney's survival in a concentration camp | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Afro-Caribbean sailor Lionel Romney survived eleven months in a concentration camp. His story illustrates how Black people were systematically persecuted under the Nazi regime.
Lionel Romney was born in Santo Domingo in 1912 and raised on Sint Maarten. As a young man, he signed on to a cargo ship to see the world. But his longing for freedom turned into a tragic odyssey. Caught up in the turmoil of World War II, his ship came under fire and sunk. The crew survived. But Lionel was taken prisoner by the Italians. After years in various camps, he was eventually deported to the Mauthausen concentration camp. He survived there for eleven months, before American troops liberated the camp. Decades after the war, Lionel Romney entrusted his memories to his daughter, Mary. Her journey from the Caribbean through Italy to Austria forms the framework of the film, which shines a light on a chapter of European history that has been suppressed to this day: the reality of life for Black people under National Socialism. This reality was marked by colonial continuities, racism, forced labor, and political arbitrariness. Lionel Romney was one of many who were exploited for propaganda purposes or subjected to persecution. Experts such as Clarence Lusane, Katharina Oguntoye, Walter Sauer, and Serge Bilé discuss historical perspectives. Archival footage and artistic reenactments weave together, in a rich visual narrative.

item.title: What happens when a blue state votes on trans sports?
item.author: Vox
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-seven Republican-controlled states have imposed measures to restrict trans athletes from playing in girls’ and women’s sports since 2020, but this November will be the first time voters have a chance to weigh in on the question directly. Ballot measures are appearing this year in Washington, Arizona, Colorado and Nebraska.
But Washington’s goes further than any other state in one key way: it would apply to all students seeking to play girls’ sports, not just athletes whose eligibility has been challenged.
The initiative, I-638, would require every girl to prove their sex assigned at birth, via “only one or more of the following: the student's reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels.”
Opponents — like Kelsey Gellner, Seattle-based pediatric nurse and board member for the Washington State Nurses Association — organizing under the NO HATE in WA State campaign, warn that the more than 150,000 school-age girls in Washington without a regular family doctor may be forced to undergo invasive genital inspections, or forgo participation in sports altogether if they can’t afford the alternative testing options.
Supporters — like Dr. Erica Li, a board-certified pediatrician in Spokane, Washington — organizing with Let's Go WA, say the fears are overblown and represent a common-sense and popular reform. Vox’s Rachel Booth talks with organizers and medical providers in Washington about what’s at stake. item.content:encoded:
Professional weightlifting requires more than raw strength. Athletes get six attempts across the snatch and clean and jerk, and the weight they declare determines when they compete. Because that number can go up but not down, lifters can disrupt an opponent’s timing, play mind games, and even miss four attempts and still win with two big lifts. #weightlifting #olympics

item.title: Men's mental health | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Mental health struggles can be hard to spot, especially among men in workplaces where strength is often associated with staying silent.
In Ireland, around one in eight male construction workers is affected by depression, and men are almost four times more likely than women to die by suicide. In Germany, the suicide rate is three times higher for men than for women.
The CAIRDE initiative in Ireland aims to encourage men working in construction to recognize early warning signs, talk openly about mental health issues, and support one another before a crisis develops.

item.title: Olympic weightlifting, explained
item.author: Vox
item.content:encoded:
Olympic weightlifting is defined by only two moves: the snatch and the clean and jerk. But behind what seems like a simple contest to see who can lift the most is a sport built on technique, speed, strategy, and psychology.
We speak to Matthew Tung, a competitive weightlifter who represents Hong Kong internationally, who breaks down how the lifts work, the strategy behind athletes changing their declared weights mid-competition, and how a lifter can miss four of their six attempts and still bring home gold.
In this video, we explore what it really takes to compete in Olympic weightlifting and what the rest of us can learn from athletes who have pushed strength training to the extreme.

item.title: An Exploration of Faith and Doubt at Ground Zero (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)
item.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
item.content:encoded:
An intimate and profound investigation of the spiritual aftershocks of the 9/11 attacks. (Aired 2002)
This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb
And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate
For many people, the most difficult questions after the deadly terror attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, were not about politics, military strategy, or homeland security. They were questions about God, evil and the potential for darkness within religion itself. And for many, those questions didn’t go away.
In “Faith and Doubt at Ground Zero,” FRONTLINE producer Helen Whitney set out to discover how the religious beliefs of Americans were challenged a year after the attacks.
From survivors who were pulled from the wreckage of the Twin Towers to the widow of a New York City firefighter; from priests and rabbis to security guards and an opera singer; from lapsed Catholics and Jews to Buddhists, Muslims, and atheists, this documentary explored and illuminated the myriad of spiritual questions that came out of the terror, pain, and destruction at Ground Zero.
“Faith and Doubt at Ground Zero” was a co-production with Helen Whitney Productions. It was written by Helen Whitney and Ron Rosenbaum. It was produced by Helen Whitney. It was reported by Leslie Berger, William Dowell, Lesley Karsten-DiNicola, and Elaine Rivera. The executive editor of FRONTLINE was Louis Wiley Jr. The executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.
In the run-up to the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, we are making a number of seminal documentaries from the days and years after 9/11 available to stream on YouTube for the first time. These documentaries offer a profound historical record of the attacks, what led up to them, the U.S. government's response, and the ripple effects across the U.S. and the world.
